verdicts.rewritten_summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum — only the 4th national vote since 1959 — which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than state-enforced) the equality settlement is.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate; Mariela Castro (CENESEX) proposed extending it to gender identity, disability and HIV status — the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators but the report makes clear passage of the SOGI ban was the confirmed outcome. Predates the 2019 Constitution/2022 Family Code (superseded in scope, not in error).

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder (wed in Ireland), the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; recaps that Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019 (later overturned on appeal, Aug 2019 — the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived). Core source for the 'recognition without status' travel posture.

Visitor-relevant: detention-placement safeguards exist at supreme-court level but practice is inconsistent.

Prison-placement risk is documented and unresolved.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: ECHR, T.H. v. the Czech Republic (App. no. 33037/22, judgment 12 Sep 2025): the Court found a violation of Article 8 regarding Czech legal-gender-recognition conditions — the surgical/sterilisation condition for official sex change and related civil-registry treatment held incompatible with private-life rights, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe as third-party interveners; the Court's reasoning frames Convention-guaranteed gender recognition through self-determination. Definitive international-law datapoint for Czech LGR posture.

Deník/ČTK (22 Jun 2018, Czech): the caretaker government backed a same-sex marriage bill introduced by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs (ANO, Pirates, KSČM, ČSSD, TOP 09, STAN) to replace registered partnerships; the Jsme fér campaign welcomed it. Dated marker of the marriage-equality legislative trail still running (per ILGA-2024, bill passed committees June 2023).

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Verfassungsblog essay (March 2026, German) 'Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern': several German states amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity; new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all; argues trans prisoners need no discriminatory special law — ordinary anti-discrimination law should govern their placement and treatment.

DW feature (23 Aug 2023): German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates — case of climate activist Penelope Frank (Last Generation), legally recorded male who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted; housing runs on a binary men/women model with gender-identity-conforming placement only exceptional.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): June — Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia 'safe countries of origin' despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there; July — Education Minister banned gender-inclusive language in her ministry, which the Federal Anti-Discrimination Office said contradicts constitutional equality protection; August — the Merz coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

BBC (20 Aug 2025): where trans far-right extremist Marla-Svenja Liebich (gender entry changed to female end-2024 under the new Self-Determination Act) would serve 18 months for incitement — Halle's chief prosecutor said Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake; press council unanimously rejected her complaint against Der Spiegel as unfounded; a Berlin court rejected her injunction against journalist Julian Reichelt.

DW (16 Jul 2026): after extradition from Czechia, Marla-Svenja Liebich was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025 — authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility; critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

Resident Advisor (20 Jun 2025): trans DJ/producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a 23 Nov 2024 Frankfurt Airport screening in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity ('targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment'); she provided RA a copy of her statement to the airport.

German STOP the HATE campaign site (Prevention & Empowerment, northern Germany): counselling-finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting ('Dunkelziffer'), evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels — a practical resource directory for someone facing hostility.

RTL (German, Jan 2025): the Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline restricting women's saunas to persons whose 'primary sex characteristics correspond' set off a debate about registered trans women's access; trans woman Alessia Dorigo countered that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic — identity is felt, not declared, and took a hard road.

Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel (German): how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women after the Self-Determination Act took effect 1 January 2025 — months of public argument over women-protected spaces with fears the self-declaration route would be misused, intensified by a Deutscher Sauna-Bund statement (paywalled body, lede captured).

Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) project page: the German penal system runs on statutory separation (§ 170(2) Lower Saxony correctional act) with binary men/women housing; placement corresponding to gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the project researches transgender people's situation in prison.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Wikipedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Djibouti SOGIESC section: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH); no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.
